Repealing minimum parking

also improving the visual
character of the downtown. It
could also result in more
efficient use of the area’s
existing parking resources.

Different land uses often
experience peak parking
demands at different times of
day and days of the week.
Shared parking can reduce the
amount of parking that needs to
be constructed, freeing up land
for more businesses, amenities,
or public space. Shared parking
encourages pedestrian activity
by allowing many small parking
facilities to be consolidated into
larger shared lots, reducing the
visual impact of surface parking
and making walking more
practical and pleasant.

• Update the development
code to establish soft
maximum parking
allowances (whereby excess
parking may be provided
only if additional TDM
measures are also
provided), equal to or based
on previous minimum
parking requirements in
code Section 17.48.040.
• Create and adopt a Parking
and TDM Plan with
requirements for the
inclusion of TDM measures
for new projects that
include more unshared
parking than allowed under
the soft maximums.

When each business or parcel
provides its own parking, the
result is often acres of
underutilized parking spaces that
sit empty much of the time.
Right-sizing parking allows more
public and private land to be
used for economic activity,
community amenities, and open
space. When developers who
wish to provide additional
parking must provide similar
benefits that will serve those
who travel by other modes, this
can support goals for community
health, social equity, and
environmental sustainability.

Strategy 1: Manage Public Parking Based on Demand
Strategy 1: Manage Public Parking Based on Demand

• Informally monitor street
parking occupancy to see
whether utilization rates
ever seem to regularly
exceed 85 percent.
• If warranted by congested
parking, conduct an initial
parking occupancy study.
• Develop a management
plan that may include time
limits, demand-based
pricing, and/or permits.
• Continually monitor
occupancy and adjust time
limits or pricing as necessary
to achieve parking
availability.

Many successful business districts
and densely developed areas
eventually find that parking
occupancies naturally come to
exceed an 85 percent threshold in
prime locations, and strategies must
be developed to maintain parking
availability. Keeping a few spaces
available on each block keeps visitors
from having to circle to find a
space—saving time, preventing
superfluous emissions, allowing
people to arrive on-time for
appointments and work, and
ensuring potential visitors do not
decide to go elsewhere due to a lack
of convenient parking.

Strategy 3: Create a Parking Benefit District

• Conduct stakeholder
outreach with the business
community.
• Establish preliminary district
boundaries.
• Establish district
membership.
• Determine the type of
governing body (e.g.,
commission, advisory board,
etc.)
• Establish roles and
responsibilities.
• Determine authority and
options for parking revenue
allocation.
• Schedule regular meetings.

When the business community and
resident stakeholders have an active
role in identifying parking issues,
needs, and opportunities, making
decisions, and allocating parking
revenue for local programs or
projects, this helps ensure that public
spaces are managed in a way that
most benefits the community, and it
helps generate buy-in and support
for parking management.

Strategy 4: Prepare to Manage Parking with Dedicated Staff

As Desert Hot Springs grows, and both the Downtown and Industrial Cannabis District are further developed, parking planning and
enforcement capabilities for on- and potentially off-street parking will be needed. Ultimately, Walker recommends that additional
staff who are dedicated to ensuring parking functionality and regulation compliance monitor parking conditions in the City, enforce
parking restrictions, and interface with private parking owners to work on a collaborative approach to providing parking.
